source_text: Θʹ. Ἔκστασις, ἔστι νεῦσις πάλιν πρὸς κακίαν λογικῆς ψυχῆς μετὰ τὴν ἀρετὴν καὶ γνῶσιν τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ. Ιʹ. Θλάσις, ἔστιν ἕξις χειρίστη λογικῆς ψυχῆς, καθ' ἢν μετέρχεται τὰς ἀρετὰς οὐ δι' αὐτὸ τὸ καλόν. ΙΑʹ. Κολόβωσις ῥινὸς, ἔστι στέρησις ἀρετῆς ἀντιλαμβανομένης εὐωδίας τῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ. ΙΒʹ. Ὠτότμησις. ἔστι σκληρία λογικῆς ψυχῆς πρὸς τὴν πνευματικὴν διδασκαλίαν ἀνθέλκουσα. ΙΓʹ. Ἐφηλὶς, ἔστι πνευματικῆς θεωρίας ἔκπτωσις, ἢ τῆς τῶν γεγονότων θεωρίας οὐκ ἀληθὴς κατανόησις. Ι∆ʹ. Μογιλαλία, ἔστι πάθος τοῦ λογιστικοῦ μέρους τῆς ψυχῆς, καθ' ὃ σκανδαλιζόμενος ἐπὶ τοῖς γινομένοις ἐν παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖν ἀδυνατεῖ τῷ Θεῷ. ΙΕʹ. Χωλότης, ἔστιν ἀδυναμία φύσεως λογικῆς πρὸς τὴν τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐργασίαν. Ιϛʹ.
thought_title: Definitions of soul-diseases nine through fifteen
orientation: Evagrius continues his numbered definitions of spiritual diseases of the rational soul, moving from ecstasy and crushing to mutilation, deafness, freckle, speech-difficulty, and lameness.
pass_a_gloss: 9. Ecstasy is a bending again toward vice of a rational soul after virtue and knowledge of God. 10. Crushing is a most wicked disposition of a rational soul, according to which it pursues the virtues not because of the beautiful itself. 11. Mutilation of the nose is a deprivation of virtue that lays hold of the fragrance of Christ. 12. Cutting off of the ear is a hardness of a rational soul toward spiritual teaching, dragging it back. 13. Freckle is a falling away from spiritual contemplation, or a not true comprehension of the contemplation of the things that have come to be. 14. Difficulty of speech is a passion of the rational soul, according to which, being scandalized at the things that happen, it is unable in everything to give thanks to God. 15. Lameness is a weakness of a rational nature toward the work of virtue.

choices.why: The standard English term for the Greek word; here it names a falling away from God after having attained virtue and knowledge, so the common rendering is kept without importing modern positive connotations.
νεῦσις is a bending or inclination; πάλιν marks the return to a former state, so 'again' is kept to preserve the temporal force.
The word means bruising or crushing; 'crushing' preserves the physical image Evagrius uses for a soul-disease.

choices.english: not because of the beautiful itself
choices.why: The phrase contrasts pursuing virtue for its own sake with pursuing it for some other motive; 'the beautiful itself' keeps the neuter substantive and the philosophical force.
The participle is active and means pulling against or dragging back; rendering it as a finite relative clause preserves the causal force of the hardness.
The noun means a falling out or away from a state; 'falling away' keeps the spatial metaphor of loss of spiritual contemplation.

pass_b_english: Ecstasy is a bending again toward vice of the rational soul, after virtue and the knowledge of God.
Crushing is a most wicked disposition of the rational soul, by which it pursues the virtues not because of the beautiful itself.
Docking of the nose is a deprivation of the virtue that takes in the fragrance of Christ.
Cutting off of the ear is a hardness of the rational soul that drags it back from spiritual teaching.
A freckle is a falling away from spiritual contemplation, or an untrue comprehension of the contemplation of the things that have come to be.
Difficulty of speech is a passion of the rational soul, by which it is scandalized at what happens and is unable to give thanks to God in everything.
Lameness is an inability of the rational nature for the work of virtue.

problems.quote: the reasoning part of the soul
problems.why: Four terms for same entity; reader may think they differ.
problems.fix: Use 'rational soul' consistently; gloss 'mind' as same.

variants.text: the reasoning part of the soul

problems.quote: the contemplation of the things that have come to be
problems.why: Reader cannot tell if these are same, subset, or distinct stages.
problems.fix: Clarify 'spiritual contemplation' = same as 'contemplation of things'.

variants.text: the contemplation of the things that have come to be

problems.why: Unclear if 'virtues of God' means God's own virtues or virtues given by God.
problems.fix: Clarify 'virtues of God' as virtues originating from God.

variants.text: virtues that contribute to the formation of Christ

problems.quote: Crushing is a most wicked disposition of the rational soul, by which it pursues the virtues not because of the beautiful itself.
problems.why: Ambiguous if this is virtue pursued for wrong motive, or pseudo-virtue.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'pursues' means 'appears to pursue' or 'pursues imperfectly'.

problems.quote: Difficulty of speech is a passion of the reasoning part of the soul, by which it is scandalized at what happens and is unable to give thanks to God in everything.
problems.why: Speech difficulty linked to scandal and ingratitude without logical connection.
problems.fix: Explain: spiritual 'dumbness' = inability to praise God amid trials.

problems.why: Same concept rendered two ways; reader may think they differ.
problems.fix: Use one term consistently or note equivalence.

problems.why: 'Scandalized' is archaic; modern reader may miss 'takes offense at events'.
problems.fix: Render as 'takes offense at what happens'.

problems.quote: not because of the beautiful itself
problems.why: 'The beautiful itself' is Platonic; modern reader may not recognize the Form of Beauty.
problems.fix: Add note: 'the beautiful itself = the Good/Beauty as such (Platonic)'.

edits.old: the reasoning part of the soul

fixed: Changed 'the reasoning part of the soul' to 'the rational soul' in both English and gloss: the source has ψυχῆς λογιστικοῦ μέρους, but the brief's glossary mandates 'rational soul' for ψυχὴ λογική, and the confirmed problem correctly notes the reader may think these are different entities.
Changed 'is scandalized at' to 'takes offense at': the source σκανδαλιζόμενος means being caused to stumble or take offense, and 'scandalized' is archaic and potentially misleading.

No edit for 'the contemplation of the things that have come to be': the source τῆς τῶν γεγονότων θεωρίας is accurately rendered, and the suggested clarification is a commentary note, not a translation fix.
No edit for 'practical virtues': the source does not contain this phrase in the given passage, so the problem is not applicable.

No edit for 'pursues the virtues not because of the beautiful itself': the source μετέρχεται τὰς ἀρετὰς οὐ δι' αὐτὸ τὸ καλόν is accurately rendered; the ambiguity is inherent in the Greek and the suggested clarification is interpretive.
No edit for 'the rational soul': the English already uses 'the rational soul' consistently in this passage.
No edit for 'not because of the beautiful itself': the source δι' αὐτὸ τὸ καλόν is accurately rendered; the Platonic resonance is intentional and the suggested note is commentary, not translation.
